title: Real Estate Lawyer Cost: Closing Attorney Fees and State Rules (2026)
description: Which states require a lawyer at closing (Georgia, North Carolina) versus custom, what a real estate lawyer charges for, and quitclaim deed costs.
h1: How much does a real estate lawyer cost?
summary: No federal rule requires a lawyer at closing, but some states do: Georgia's Supreme Court requires a licensed Georgia attorney to close transactions and facilitate deed execution, and North Carolina law treats deed preparation and title opinions as the practice of law. Elsewhere lawyers are optional or customary. Fees are often flat for routine closings; as an illustration, 4 hours at Clio's $349 national average rate is $1,396.
body:
Is a lawyer required at a real estate closing?

There is no federal rule requiring a lawyer to close a home purchase. Whether you need one depends on your state, and it helps to separate three different situations.

1. Required by a court ruling or statute

  • Georgia: the Supreme Court of Georgia held in 2003 that it is the unauthorized practice of law for anyone other than a licensed Georgia attorney to close a real estate transaction or to prepare or facilitate the execution of a deed for a seller, borrower or lender. The court rejected "witness-only" closings run by non-lawyers [1].
  • North Carolina: state law defines the practice of law to include preparing deeds and mortgages and "abstracting or passing upon titles," so those tasks must be done by a lawyer when performed for others. Real estate brokers may only fill in preprinted forms under Real Estate Commission rules [2].

2. Customary but not required

In some states and regions, buyers and sellers usually hire lawyers by local custom even though no rule requires it. In others, title or escrow companies commonly run the closing and a lawyer is brought in only when there is a problem. Custom is not law: if your state does not require a lawyer, you can choose whether to hire one.

3. Not verified here

Published lists of "attorney states" often also include South Carolina, Massachusetts, Delaware, Connecticut, New York, West Virginia and others. Those lists mix court rulings, bar opinions and custom, and some rules have changed. We could not confirm the current rule for those states from a primary source as of October 2026, so we do not label them required or customary. Ask your state bar or your lender's closing department what applies to your transaction.

What a real estate lawyer does and what you pay for

Real estate lawyers usually charge a flat fee for a standard residential closing and bill hourly for problems or for commercial work. We have not found a reliable national survey of closing fees, so we explain the components and illustrate the time with Clio's national average rate of $349 an hour [4].

  • Contract review or drafting: especially important in for-sale-by-owner deals, new construction and contracts with unusual contingencies.
  • Title review: reviewing the title search and commitment, and clearing liens, judgments or boundary issues.
  • Deed and document preparation: preparing the deed and other closing documents, which some states reserve to lawyers [1][2].
  • Running the closing: explaining documents, handling the escrow money and recording the deed.
  • Representing the lender: in many attorney-closing transactions the lawyer's fee appears on your Closing Disclosure even though the lawyer represents the lender or acts as settlement agent, not you. Ask who the lawyer represents.

Example (hourly illustration): reviewing a purchase contract (1 hour), title issues (1.5 hours) and attending the closing (1.5 hours) = 4 hours × $349 [4] = $1,396. A clean transaction handled on a flat fee may cost less; a title defect or a dispute with the seller can add many hours.

What drives the cost up

  • Who the lawyer represents. A lawyer for the buyer only is a different engagement from a settlement attorney who also works for the lender.
  • Transaction type. Cash purchases, refinances, for-sale-by-owner sales and commercial property each involve different work.
  • Title problems. Unreleased mortgages, missing heirs, liens and survey disputes take time to clear.
  • Negotiation. Repair credits, delayed closings and contract disputes are usually billed hourly.
  • Estate and family transfers. Transferring property from an estate, between relatives or into a trust adds probate or trust questions; see estate planning lawyer cost.

Attorney fees are only one line of closing costs. Your lender must give you a Closing Disclosure listing your total closing costs three business days before closing [3]. Compare the attorney or settlement fee there with what you were quoted, and ask about anything you do not recognize.

Quitclaim deeds and simple transfers

A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the signer has, with no promise that the title is good. It is commonly used between spouses, family members or into a trust, not for sales to strangers. Preparing your own deed is generally permitted, but in states such as Georgia and North Carolina, preparing deeds for other people is the practice of law [1][2]. Before recording a self-prepared deed, check the county recorder's formatting rules and transfer-tax forms, and consider whether the transfer affects your mortgage, title insurance or property tax.

Questions to ask a real estate lawyer

  • Do you represent me, the lender, or both?
  • Is the closing a flat fee? What is included, and what is billed hourly?
  • Are title search, title insurance and recording fees included or separate?
  • Will you review the purchase contract before I sign it?
  • What happens to the fee if the deal falls through?

Related: landlord-tenant lawyer cost, notary fees and hourly vs flat fees.

faq.q: Which states require a lawyer for a real estate closing?
faq.a: Georgia's Supreme Court requires a licensed Georgia attorney to close transactions and facilitate deed execution, and North Carolina law treats preparing deeds and passing on title as the practice of law. Several other states are often listed as attorney states, but the rules vary and should be confirmed with the state bar.

faq.q: Does the closing attorney represent me?
faq.a: Not necessarily. In many transactions the settlement attorney is hired by or represents the lender. If you want advice on your own interests, ask the lawyer in writing whom they represent or hire your own.

faq.q: How much does a real estate lawyer charge?
faq.a: Residential closings are often flat-fee and other work hourly. As an illustration, 4 hours at Clio's $349 national average is $1,396, but local flat fees can differ widely, so get written quotes.

faq.q: Can I prepare my own quitclaim deed?
faq.a: Owners can generally prepare their own deeds, but preparing deeds for others is reserved to lawyers in states such as Georgia and North Carolina. Check your county recorder's requirements before recording.
